To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the accuracy of a classifier is not only a function of the training algorithm and the classification family, but also of the dataset used for training.

the optimal classifier is obtained by using the simplest possible method, that is, the one that requires the smallest number of experiments, and that the accuracy of a classification method depends only on the number of experiments used to train it.

(1) inductive learning methods that minimize classification errors are not consistent, (2) inductive learning algorithms that are consistent do not minimize classification errors, and (3) the optimal classification system for a given problem is the one that minimizes the expected classification error.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a classification system with high accuracy when only a small number of experiments is available and the domain knowledge of the system designer is limited.

the following issues: a) the design of a classification system based on a consistent learning method, b) the design of reduced data sets for accuracy estimation, and c) the design of accuracy estimators for classification systems.
the design of inductive learning systems with optimal performance, when the available experimental data is small.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in order to obtain a reliable and accurate classification system, it is necessary to carefully select a classification family, to design a consistent training algorithm and to use a proper accuracy estimator.

, in the presence of a small number of available experiments and of limited domain knowledge, the system designer should be satisfied with a simple, consistent, and well understood inductive learning system, such as a nearest neighbor rule, rather than with a more complex and less well understood system, such as, for instance, a neural network.

(1) a consistent classification algorithm is always preferable to a non-consistent algorithm, (2) a consistent algorithm is always preferable when the number of training samples is small, (3) the accuracy of a consistent algorithm does not depend on the classification family used to build the classifier, (4) the use of different classification families is justified by different levels of accuracy in different problem domains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best accuracy is achieved by using a small number of experiments and the most simple classification method, provided that a suitable dataset is available.
the best accuracy is obtained by a simple algorithm, based on a simple classification family, and that this algorithm is robust against the presence of noise in the training set.

, for a given problem, there is no reason to believe that a classification system with higher accuracy can be designed by increasing the amount of data, the number of training algorithms, the complexity of the learning methods, and the number of classification families.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of the classification method is a crucial design decision, whose impact is often underestimated.

a simple, consistent, and computationally inexpensive algorithm, such as a decision tree, can achieve the same level of accuracy as a more complex and expensive algorithm, such as support vector machines, when the available data is scarce and the underlying problem is not very difficult.
the system designer should focus on a small number of consistent classification algorithms with a well understood behavior, rather than on a large number of inconsistent ones.
